lines.text: The Middle Ages.
The period between 500 and 1500 AD is called the Middle Ages [middeleeuwen].
Back then there were small territories, each with its own leader.
These territories were called 'de Nederlanden'.
The word 'Nederland' means: the low land [het lage land].
Almost everyone belonged to the Roman Catholic Church [rooms-katholieke kerk].
The church had a lot of power [macht].
The Eighty Years' War.
In the sixteenth century (1500–1600) many people wanted to start their own churches: Protestant [protestantse] churches.
The Netherlands belonged to Spain [Spanje] at that time.
The Spanish king was Roman Catholic and said that all Protestants had to die.
The people rose up in resistance [verzet].
This is how a war [oorlog] began in 1568 that lasted eighty years.
Willem van Oranje was a political leader in the Netherlands.
He believed that everyone should be allowed to have their own faith.
He became Protestant and became the leader of the resistance against Spain.
In 1584 Willem van Oranje was shot dead [doodgeschoten] in his house in Delft.
You can still visit that house today.
Willem van Oranje was the ancestor [voorvader] of King Willem-Alexander.
That is why the king is also called 'Willem'.
And orange [oranje] is still an important color for the Netherlands: athletes often wear orange clothing at international competitions.
Trade in the seventeenth century.
The war against Spain lasted until 1648.
In the seventeenth century (1600–1700) the Netherlands became very rich through trade [handel].
The Dutch sailed ships all over the world.
They bought and sold goods, for example gold and spices [specerijen].
But they also sold people: these people had been made into a slave [slaaf].
Colonies.
The Netherlands acquired colonies [koloniën], for example South Africa, Indonesia [Indonesië] (formerly: the Dutch East Indies) and later Suriname.
They paid nothing for the goods from the colonies.
The enslaved people had to work there on plantations [plantages].
The Dutch earned a lot of money from this.
Canal houses and art.
Rich people had expensive houses built along a canal [gracht].
You can still see such canal houses [grachtenhuizen] in old cities like Amsterdam and Utrecht.
Art became important: rich people commissioned paintings [schilderijen].
A famous painter from that time is Rembrandt, for example with *De Nachtwacht*.
The Second World War.
In 1933 Hitler gained a lot of power in Germany.
His soldiers began to occupy [bezetten] other countries.
The Netherlands was occupied in 1940 within five days.
The center of Rotterdam was almost completely destroyed by bombs at that time.
The winter of 1944 is called the Hunger Winter [Hongerwinter]: there was too little food and it was very cold.
Many people died.
The Holocaust.
Hitler said that the economic problems were caused by the Jews [Joden].
Jews were given fewer and fewer rights [rechten] and had to wear a Jewish star [Jodenster] on their clothes.
Later, Jews had to go by train to camps in Germany and Poland.
There they died of hunger and disease or in gas chambers [gaskamers].
Many Jews went to live in a secret place: this is called going into hiding [onderduiken].
The murder of six million Jews is called the Holocaust.
Anne Frank, a thirteen-year-old Jewish girl, had to go into hiding with her family in Amsterdam in 'het Achterhuis'.
She wrote a famous diary [dagboek].
She was captured and died in a German camp.
Het Achterhuis is now a museum.
Antisemitism [Antisemitisme] is discrimination against Jewish people.
That is forbidden [verboden] under Dutch law.
The liberation.
The United States, Canada, England and the Soviet Union fought together against Germany.
In 1945 Germany lost the war.
From 5 May 1945 the Netherlands was free again.
That is why there is Remembrance of the Dead [Dodenherdenking] on 4 May and Liberation Day [Bevrijdingsdag] on 5 May.
Migrants.
Different groups came to the Netherlands:
People from the former colonies: Indonesia became free in 1949, Suriname in 1975.
Guest workers [Gastarbeiders]: around 1970 the economy was doing well.
People from Turkey, Morocco and Southern Europe came here to work.
They were supposed to stay temporarily [tijdelijk], but many of their children and grandchildren still live here.
Labor migrants [Arbeidsmigranten] and knowledge/skilled migrants [kennismigranten]: labor migrants often come from Eastern Europe and work, for example, in construction.
Expats or knowledge migrants have a theoretical (higher) education, come for example from India, and often work in ICT or for a university.
Refugees [Vluchtelingen]: people who have fled [gevlucht] from countries with war or political problems, for example Syria, Turkey, Iran, Eritrea or Yemen.
Cooperation with other countries.
In the United Nations (UN) [Verenigde Naties (VN)], countries from all over the world work together for peace [vrede] and security [veiligheid].
UN soldiers protect areas where there are conflicts.
NATO [NAVO] is a military alliance [militaire samenwerking] of countries in Europe, the United States and Canada.
The EU [Europese Unie] is an economic cooperation [economische samenwerking] of countries in Europe.
